argument: Nishitani argues that every common definition of religion, from the atheist's security blanket to the scholar's relationship to an absolute, shares the same flaw: it frames religion from the outside in terms of its utilitarian function, which is exactly the mode of thinking a real religious quest has to move beyond. A true religious quest begins when a person stops asking what use things serve to them and starts asking for what purpose they exist, moving from the field of consciousness, through an honest confrontation with nihility, toward sunyata, where self and world are experienced as co-constituting rather than separate. Because this quest requires engaging with nihilism rather than being distracted from it, shallow mass-produced religion turns out to be anti-religious, while Nietzsche's declaration that God is dead, by forcing modern people to start from an existential confrontation with nihilism, actually foreshadows a possible golden age of religious participation.
keyIdeas: All the surveyed definitions of religion, from the atheist to the churchgoer to the scholars, share one flaw: they describe religion from the outside in terms of its utilitarian function, what use it serves a person or society.
A truly religious quest begins with a shift from asking what use does this serve to me toward asking for what purpose do I exist within the larger network of being.

Like a university that most people use shallowly but that remains one of the only places capable of producing a rare transformation, religion should not be abandoned as a word or a path just because most people engage with it superficially; shallow mass-produced religion, by distracting people from nihilism, even ends up blocking religious questions and becomes anti-religious.

Nishitani maps experience onto three fields of awareness, consciousness, nihility, and sunyata, and the religious quest is the movement from the dualistic, reifying field of consciousness through nihility to sunyata; the appearance of nihility is not a bad thing but a sign that awareness of self-existence has reached extraordinary depth.

Instead of reifying or nullifying the self, Nishitani proposes emptying it of the artifacts of consciousness, as in Simone Weil's example of truly receiving another person in conversation, so that we become like an antenna for the universe, and because sunyata is immanent rather than transcendent, the goal is to remove our projections and notice what is already part of experience, arriving at the real self-realization of reality in which we actualize and understand reality at once.

terms.def: The representational field of awareness where a subject relates to objects it tries to reify and control, the dualistic, utilitarian standpoint where most people spend nearly their whole lives.

The field of awareness encountered when that which undermines the stable meanings we use to make sense of reality emerges, rendering life's meaning meaningless and turning our existence into a question mark.
The immanent field of awareness, the groundless ground or emptiness, in which the illusion of separation dissolves and self and world are experienced as co-constituting on their own home ground.
The practice of emptying the self of the artifacts of consciousness, not nullifying it, in order to liberate it and open room to notice sunyata as it is always already there.
Nishitani's phrase, exploiting the double meaning of realization in English, for how in sunyata we simultaneously actualize reality and understand it as our being unfolds.
